summary: This informational memo describes ways an internet service provider can add IPv6 to an existing IPv4 network without disrupting IPv4 service. It analyses the scenarios, evaluates how useful the existing transition mechanisms are in each, and points out known challenges.

eli5.summary: A town with only old roads wants to add a new set of roads without closing the old ones. This document looks at ways a network company can do that.

ipv6 transition scenarios for service providers
how do isps deploy ipv6 alongside ipv4

how can an isp upgrade the backbone versus customer connections first
what tunneling techniques are used during ipv6 transition
subtitle: Adding IPv6 service to an ISP without disrupting existing IPv4.

tldr.problem: Internet Service Providers running IPv4 networks need to add IPv6 service, but cannot simply replace IPv4 overnight. The path forward depends on a provider's network architecture and customer needs.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes phased transition scenarios (Launch, Backbone-first, Customer-first, Complete) and detailed actions for upgrading backbone and customer-facing network components to support both IPv4 and IPv6 natively or via tunneling.
tldr.outcome: ISPs now have a blueprint for IPv6 deployment matching their topology and risk tolerance, covering backbone transition, customer connection upgrades, authentication, management, and operational concerns.

today: RFC 4029 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary reference for ISP-scale IPv6 deployment planning. Most large ISPs have by now completed Stage 3 (full dual-stack), but many still use the framework from this RFC to evaluate new access technologies and regional rollouts.

sections.title: The IPv6 Deployment Challenge
sections.content:
IPv6 deployment in ISP networks is not a flag-flip operation. An Internet Service Provider must add IPv6 connectivity and address space to its customers while leaving existing IPv4 service untouched. This document addresses a dual-stack network – one natively supporting both IPv4 and IPv6.

The challenge is scope: ISP networks include backbone routers, customer connection networks (from the provider edge to customer premises), network operations (management, billing, accounting), and peering relationships with other providers. Upgrading all these pieces at once is expensive and risky. The RFC proposes a phased approach where different parts of the network upgrade at different times.

The ISP's goal is to offer both IPv4 and IPv6 service to customers. Depending on network architecture and risk tolerance, an ISP may upgrade the backbone first, the customer-facing networks first, or both simultaneously.
sections.eli5: A network provider needs to add IPv6 to its infrastructure without breaking IPv4. Different parts of the network can upgrade at different times depending on the provider's choices.

sections.title: ISP Network Components and Stages
sections.content:
A typical ISP network divides into three parts: backbone (core routers, border routers for peering), customer connection networks (provider edge equipment and last-hop links to customer premises), and network and service operations (management, billing, customer service systems).

The RFC identifies four stages of IPv6 maturity:

Stage 1 (Launch): IPv4-only ISP with IPv4-only customers. The first step is obtaining IPv6 prefix allocation from a Regional Internet Registry and establishing IPv6 connectivity to upstream providers and peers.

Stage 2a (Backbone): The backbone supports both IPv4 and IPv6, but customer connection networks remain IPv4-only. IPv6 is delivered to customers via tunnels through the IPv4 access network.

Stage 2b (Customer Connection): The backbone remains IPv4-only, but customer connection networks are upgraded to dual-stack. IPv6 traffic is tunneled across the IPv4 backbone or carried in a separate overlay network.

Stage 3 (Complete): Both backbone and customer connection networks are fully dual-stack, with native IPv6 support throughout.

ISPs can follow different paths: Stage 2a then 3, Stage 2b then 3, or Stage 2 and 3 combined. No single path is mandatory.
sections.eli5: An ISP network has three parts. Each can upgrade to IPv6 in different orders. Upgrade the core first, the edges first, or both together – there is no wrong choice, only different costs and risks.

sections.title: Backbone Transition Strategy
sections.content:
For ISPs choosing a backbone-first approach, the transition can follow intermediate steps. The backbone can start with tunnels or dedicated IPv6-only links connecting a few routers, then gradually add dual-stack routers until the entire backbone supports both protocols natively.

For ISPs with MPLS-based backbones, IPv6 support requires additional choices: native dual-stack routing, IPv6 label switched paths, or IPv6-over-MPLS tunneling. Native dual-stack is ideal but requires the most equipment investment. IPv6 LSPs require control-plane upgrades. Tunneling is the quickest interim step but may not scale to very large networks.

Routing protocols must also support IPv6: either OSPFv3 or IS-IS for interior routing, and BGP with multiprotocol extensions for exterior routing. Many ISPs run separate IPv4 and IPv6 routing processes initially for isolation, then consolidate to a single process as IPv6 stabilizes.

Peering with other ISPs can be established natively over IPv6 (recommended) or via tunnels (temporary measure). Internet exchanges increasingly offer native IPv6 peering infrastructure.
sections.eli5: To upgrade a backbone, start small with a few IPv6-capable routers connected by tunnels, then add more until everything speaks IPv6. Choose routing protocols that work with IPv6.

sections.title: Customer Connection Transition and Access Technologies
sections.content:
Customer connection networks face different challenges. Small customer sites (home users, small businesses) may use simple tunneling mechanisms like configured tunnels with a tunnel broker, 6to4 relays, or Teredo. Large sites with managed networks often prefer dual-stack access or static configured tunnels.

Dynamic IPv4 address allocation complicates tunneling. If a customer's IPv4 address changes frequently, the tunnel endpoint address becomes unstable. Solutions include tunnel brokering services that auto-update the tunnel configuration, or protocols like DHCPv6 prefix delegation that assign stable IPv6 prefixes independent of the IPv4 address.

Layer 2 access technologies (like xDSL or Ethernet) need only provider edge upgrades if they are transparent to IP. Layer 3 awareness (like layer 3 switches in fiber-to-the-home access) requires more careful integration with authentication, DHCP snooping, and access control.

For customer equipment (CPE), either the CPE must support IPv6 natively, or the provider must host a tunnel endpoint (like a tunnel broker or IPv6 relay). Terminating tunnels at the CPE is preferable when possible because it avoids NAT and firewall traversal issues.
sections.eli5: To reach customers, the ISP can upgrade their last-hop networks or use tunnels. Small customers might use simple tunnels; big customers might get native IPv6. Either way, the ISP must choose where the IPv6 connection starts (at customer gear or in the provider's equipment).

sections.title: Operations: Management, Traceability, and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Operational concerns include prefix delegation (DHCPv6 must assign IPv6 prefixes to customers, not just addresses), authentication (RADIUS and other systems must support IPv6), traceability and logging (the ISP must map IPv6 addresses and prefixes to customers for abuse reporting), and ingress filtering (networks must validate that packets claiming to come from a customer actually originate from that customer).

Quality of Service (QoS) systems designed for IPv4 must be updated. Many bandwidth provisioning systems assume IPv4 addresses; they must be taught to handle IPv6 prefixes. DiffServ works for IPv6 as well as IPv4, but configuration tools may need upgrades.

Network management is initially possible over IPv4 transport (using IPv6 MIBs), but monitoring functions using ICMPv6 (like ping or traceroute) require native IPv6 transport. Multihoming (customers connecting to multiple ISPs) requires mechanisms to choose which ISP's IPv6 prefix to use for outbound traffic – this is still evolving and a topic of ongoing IETF work.
sections.eli5: Beyond connecting IPv6, the ISP must update all its operational tools: customer service systems, billing, security checks, and quality controls must all understand IPv6.
